page.title: How to Host Virtual Events Guide
page.description: Step‑by‑step checklist for planning, producing and following up virtual events, with tool categories, timelines and production tips and budget considerations.
page.definition: Virtual event hosting is the end‑to‑end process of selecting a platform, designing a run of show, managing registration, rehearsing speakers, broadcasting live with a backup stream, recording the session and delivering follow‑up assets to attendees including post‑event analytics and content repurposing.
page.quick_answer: Pick a platform that matches your audience size, build a run of show with a designated producer, run a full rehearsal on the live system two to five days before, and send the replay within twenty‑four to forty‑eight hours.

sections.h2: What platform should I choose for a virtual event?

blocks.p: Choose a platform that matches your attendee capacity, interaction needs and budget model. The market offers three cost models: per‑host licences sized by attendee capacity such as Zoom Webinars, self‑serve monthly plans like StreamYard and Livestorm, and annual contracts quoted by sales for suites such as ON24, Cvent, Bizzabo and Goldcast. Ten platforms compared below range from self‑serve streaming studios to enterprise event suites.

sections.h2: How do I build a run of show and assign owners?

blocks.p: Create a run of show that breaks the event into timed segments and assigns a single owner to each segment. Seven stages each with one owner and one output guide the workflow: intake, brief, production, review, approval, publishing and reporting.

ol: Intake – gather goals, audience size and date
Brief – write speaker briefs, slide templates and run of show
Production – rehearse on the live platform, test backup stream
Review – collect feedback from producer and speakers
Approval – sign off final assets and schedule
Publishing – push registration page, calendar invites and reminders
Reporting – deliver attendance, engagement and replay metrics

sections.h2: What production crew do I need for a webinar versus a summit?

blocks.p: A simple webinar can be run by one producer while a summit or hybrid event requires a show caller, speaker manager, moderator and platform operator. The table below maps typical roles to each format.

sections.h2: How do I manage registration, engagement and follow‑up?

blocks.p: Set up registration, live engagement tools and a follow‑up workflow before the event goes live. A checklist keeps every item visible and owned.

ul: Registration platform (Eventbrite or Cvent) with confirmation email
Reminder schedule at two weeks, one week and one day before
Live Q&A tool and poll tool enabled in the platform
Chat moderation assigned to a dedicated moderator
Replay delivery within twenty‑four to forty‑eight hours
Post‑event survey link in the follow‑up email
CRM sync of attendee data to HubSpot or Salesforce

sections.h2: What timeline and budget should I expect?

blocks.p: Plan a webinar three to four weeks out and a summit six to eight weeks out, with production costs ranging from a few thousand for a moderated webinar to tens of thousands for a full conference.

Moderated webinars: $2,500 to $7,500 per production (West Peek Productions published range, directional, not a fixed quote). Executive summits, online conferences and hybrid productions: $10,000 to $50,000 and above (West Peek Productions published range). West Peek Productions produces virtual, hybrid and webinar events and sets up marketing, content and creative operations.

faq.q: How far in advance should I book a platform?
faq.a: Reserve the platform at least six weeks before a summit and three weeks before a webinar; this gives time for contract review, branding setup and a full technical rehearsal on the live system and to confirm backup streaming options early.

faq.q: What is the difference between a platform licence and a production crew?
faq.a: A platform licence provides the streaming software and attendee access, while a production crew supplies the run of show, camera operators, encoder, backup stream and live direction; both purchases are required for a polished event and ensures redundancy during live broadcast.

faq.q: When should I send the replay to attendees?
faq.a: Deliver the edited recording within twenty‑four to forty‑eight hours after the session ends, while the content is still fresh and before the next communication cycle begins. Include a short highlight clip and a link to the on‑demand library for easy access.

faq.q: Do I need a backup stream for every virtual event?
faq.a: Yes, a secondary stream protects against primary encoder failure, network outage or platform glitch; assign a platform operator to monitor both feeds and switch instantly if the main feed drops. This redundancy is standard for professional productions and adds minimal cost.
